event: VXE 889 lost downlink in flight at Twentynine Palms and, because LandOnError=1 was set in gcs.ini, was commanded to land immediately and was lost (splash) on range R106.
failure_mode: loss of downlink; GCS setting LandOnError=1 turned the link loss into an immediate land command instead of a lost-link return
contributing: gcs.ini LandOnError=1 enabled with no indication to the operator, probably changed by a person
GCS log shows the GCS main loop blocked for about 35 s just before the loss of downlink warning
aircraft could not be nudged during the land immediately

evidence.quote: LandOnError=1 is enabled in the gcs.ini
From the logs I can see that the vehicle lost communications and was commanded to Land Immediately.
[09:51:24.765] MessageBoxTop(): LOSS OF DOWNLINK LANDING
Interesting to note that gcs.ini is not corrupt in other ways previously seen.
Here is the incident report for the VXE-30 Stalker splash last night on R106

team_view_in_comments: Ted discovered ini had been changed. Probable cause Operator Error

would_settle_it.what: XCOMM and radio logs at the loss of downlink, to see whether the link dropped at the aircraft, the radio or the stalled GCS
FTP logs from the aircraft covering the incident flight and the gcs.ini history
operator event summary (not converted, cut off in the email)

reasoning: The GCS log shows a loss of downlink warning followed by LOSS OF DOWNLINK LANDING, and Ted found LandOnError=1 set in gcs.ini, so the land immediately was the configured response to a real link loss. Why the downlink was lost is not shown; the GCS main loop was blocked for about 35 s right before the warning, which points at either the GCS or the link. The evidence therefore gets to the downlink as the degraded input, with the ini setting as the reason the response ended in a crash.
notes: No Root Cause field; the Executive Summary says operator error. The only AAR pack listed is dated 260624 while the email refers to an incident on 07-15-26, so the pack may not be the incident flight. The email's incident report spreadsheet was not converted. Stephan notes the attached investigation is not readable.

event: VXE 525 (with center wing 876, HD45 battery) nose-dived shortly after transition to fixed-wing flight and was destroyed.
failure_mode: indicated airspeed stayed low (about 25.7 fps) while GPS ground speed rose to 74 fps during transition; pitot system found leaking significantly after the crash
contributing: HLB cell failure seen in the same flight
low preflight pitot push reading (55 fps)

evidence.quote: @Alexander Alan Arnold @David Grosher the xcomm logs show a ground speed of 74fps while the airspeed is only 25.7fps just before the logs cut.
on the transition the airspeed just never really increased while groundspeed did.  This to me points to an issue with the pitot.
Confirmed pitot system is leaking significantly but unable to reasonably conclude if issue occurred pre or post incident.
Coincidentally, this aircraft appears to have had an HLB cell failure during the issue that Eric reported as well.

team_view_in_comments: it seems like a reasonable conclusion to suspect the airspeed as root cause.

would_settle_it.what: airspeed versus ground speed through transition
air data pod inspection photos and where the pitot leak is, to judge pre-crash versus impact damage
timing of the HLB cell failure relative to the nose dive

reasoning: XCOMM logs show indicated airspeed not rising during transition while GPS ground speed rose to 74 fps in light winds, which points to a wrong airspeed reading rather than a real low airspeed. The returned air data pod had a significant pitot leak, but engineering could not tell whether it was there before the crash. An HLB cell failure in the same flight is a second candidate, so the evidence gets to the air data system as the most likely start but not to one proven part.
notes: No Root Cause field. RMA-1091 holds intake forms and photos only; the intake form text is blank, the packing slip is image only, and the customer RMA text says a system hardware issue caused a battery issue. RMA-224 (2024 RMA on the same tail) was not read as it predates this incident.

event: VXE 885 flew erratically (rolls and dives) while loitering in fixed-wing flight and crashed, a total loss.
failure_mode: excess solder flux under the RF shield cover burned and caused leakage currents and a short; in flight the fixed-wing pitch gyro had a bias over 10 deg/s and then froze for tens of seconds
contributing: no preflight gyro bias limit to flag the bad gyro
fail-safe kept trying to recover fixed-wing control instead of landing

evidence.quote: The gyro bias of the fixed-wing pitch gyro is over 10 degrees per second for most fo the flight, and then around the time of the attitude divergence the gyro reading is constant for tens of seconds.
A fresh mag/accel board was then soldered on to the original #885 FWAP and re-tested on the same av box.
The cover was cut off of the #885 mag/accel board and it was observed there was an excess of flux covering the circuitry (see photos below).
On this board, the burned flux caused a short circuit.
The fact that a processor does not work as expected following a crash does not mean that it was the root cause of a crash.

team_view_in_comments: Root cause determined as excess flux on mag/accel board and internal report available for review.

would_settle_it.what: fixed-wing pitch gyro bias and the frozen gyro output during the attitude divergence
full teardown and swap test record, and whether the flux short explains the in-flight gyro bias

attachments_read: 64373_885 CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form V885 260831-1.pdf.md
64494_885 CF-855-001 Return Material Authorization (RMA) Request Form V885 AND EPS6516.pdf.md
reasoning: Flight logs show the fixed-wing pitch gyro with a large bias and then a frozen output at the time of the attitude divergence. Swap tests moved the dead-sensor fault with the 885 mag/accel board, a fresh board cured it, and cleaning excess flux from under the shield made the 885 board work again. That ties the fault to the mag/accel board and a build flux defect, though, as Dave Grosher noted, post-crash behaviour does not by itself prove the in-flight cause, so confidence is medium.
notes: No Root Cause field; the conclusion is in Issue Status. An earlier claim of microcontroller breakdown was withdrawn after the swap tests. RMA-1100 intake PDF (named 883 intake) has no text. RMA-1104 is the damaged gimbal, not causal. ENG-1750 confirms the MPU-9250 sits on the Mag Accel 2 board 107-103101.

event: VXE 1034 pitched up and rolled right at about 100 ft during VTOL takeoff when the rear right lift prop stopped, then descended rapidly with uncommanded yaw and crashed.
failure_mode: rear right lift prop stopped in climb while motor 3 throttle was commanded high (loss of thrust on motor 3)
contributing: operator commanded a VTOL abort after the initial upset
ground crew approached before motors were safe

evidence.quote: the back right lift prop stop spinning and av lost control and hit the ground
AAR data confirms at ~100ft a pitch up and roll right (uncommanded) followed by rapid descent in VTOL with uncommanded yaw.
Motor 3 throttle is sustained high when issue occurs. Indicating motor 3 (rear right motor) is likely the cause of issue.
HLB cell balances look normal

team_view_in_comments: Motor 3 throttle is sustained high when issue occurs. Indicating motor 3 (rear right motor) is likely the cause of issue.

event: VXE 863 lost link about 1.5 hours into a Border Patrol flight, the fixed-wing control froze, and the aircraft nose-dived into the ground and was destroyed.
component: XCOMM CycloneTCP network stack (nicSendPacket infinite wait)
failure_mode: a network transmit wait with infinite timeout held the network mutex, locking XCOMM communication tasks; FWAP telemetry and uplink stopped and the vehicle dove
contributing: no timeout or recovery path for an Ethernet transmit stall
unclear whether 863 hardware made the stall more likely

evidence.quote: The data seems to indicate fixed-wing became unresponsive and likely cut all the actuators which led to a nose dive.
With some help from John and Scott we were able to identify that few software tasks were blocked due to an infinite wait time and the innards of our communication software being locked up.
FWAP sensors populate and respond to avionics movement. FWAP versions populate on xcomm throughput.
at this point it’s looking like just a really infrequent corner case of the software that can cause this vs. something inherently wrong with 863’s hardware.
though better than the vehicle-863 freeze case (which required a physical power cycle).
this one can be prioritized ahead of that overall effort since it crashed a plane.

team_root_cause: Software tasks on xcomm locked due to infinite block inside CycloneTCP.  Unclear if hardware made this software failure mode more likely to happen.

would_settle_it.what: the TRACE evidence tying the freeze to the nicSendPacket wait on the incident flight

reasoning: Logs show all FWAP telemetry on XCOMM froze while BMS data kept updating, and the vehicle then dove. Engineering traced this to software tasks blocked on an infinite wait inside the CycloneTCP stack, and the FS2-5173 analysis names the nicSendPacket transmit wait with NIC_MAX_BLOCKING_TIME left at infinite. Post-crash bench tests showed XCOMM and FWAP communicating and a week-long soak did not repeat it, so a hardware cause looks unlikely but is not ruled out.
notes: FS2-5173 says both XCOMM and the autopilot share the same stack defect. RMA-1082 attachments are a duplicate maintenance log, an image-only intake, and an OCR'd January 2026 RMA traveler package from the earlier VXEP-1548 glide landing repair; I read pages 1 to 46 of that OCR text and skipped the remainder (build travelers, not cause related). Comment notes the requested board swap was not done in that earlier RMA.

event: On the ground during Launch Wizard motor tests after a normal flight, the rear left lift motor of VXE 1021 did not respond to spin commands; all four spun on later retest.
component: VTOL AP motor test command handling
failure_mode: motor test commands reached XCOMM but did not produce a spin; VTOL AP silently ignores a same-motor test request while an override is already active
contributing: operator sent repeated motor 4 test commands less than 5 s apart
XCOMM CSV sampling gaps of about 10 s hide short tests

evidence.quote: Ran the VTOL Motors while on ground, all 4 spun as expected.
There are 0 instances when the motor/ESC didnt respond to a given command according to ESC logs
If row 9 reached and activated the VTOL override, row 10 would therefore be silently ignored rather than extending or restarting the test.
A closer analysis of the 1021 data shows there’s no smoking gun in the motor tests that weren’t responded to.

team_view_in_comments: Hardware is currently assessed as healthy.

would_settle_it.what: VTOL AP log of motor test acceptance or denial for each RCS_MOTOR command
outcome of the V974 investigation of the same symptom

reasoning: The rear left ESC logs show every command it received was acted on, and the motor spun normally on retest, so the ESC and motor look healthy. Scott Hunter's write-up shows XCOMM forwarded every request and that the VTOL AP silently ignores a repeat test on a motor whose test is still active, while the slow CSV sampling explains most apparent misses. That narrows the no-spin to the command path in the VTOL AP motor test handling, without proof of which commands were dropped.
notes: Issue Status says root cause not yet identified; Executive Summary says probable operator error. ESC log header shows 766 corrupt points. The XKIT-5382 attachment is the same write-up as this ticket's. Same symptom on V974 (front left then back right) in XKIT-5382.

event: On the ground, VXE 1003 (fuel cell, OGCS) reported 24.52 kg of fuel at power up and 4.04 kg after a reset instead of the 970 g the operator entered.
failure_mode: VSM builds its own fuel remaining from the user-entered initial fuel and burn rate and does not read the embedded fuel state; after a VSM reset the initial fuel value is wrongly initialized (likely an uninitialized variable)
contributing: fuel system design does not use the embedded initial fuel state

evidence.quote: After an investigation it doesn’t look like xcomm was confused about the fuel remaining, and the error only shows momentarily after vsm resets.
Best hypothesis I have is an uninitialized variable picking up some junk
VSM appears to construct its own fuel remaining status from a user entered initial fuel and then a GBurn rate.
The errant values don’t occur in the xcomm datalogs.

team_view_in_comments: After many rounds of investigating I’m pretty sure this is isolated to the VSM, because the VSM doesn’t currently consume the initial fuel system state from the embedded side.

would_settle_it.what: full investigation notes isolating the fault to the VSM code
test on the aircraft that the erroneous fuel value no longer appears after reset

reasoning: XCOMM datalogs never show the wrong fuel values, while the VSM is shown to build its own fuel remaining from the user entry, so the error comes from the VSM. The exact mechanism (an uninitialized initial fuel value after reset) is the developer's best hypothesis and the fix is untested, so confidence is medium.
notes: No Root Cause field. XKIT-5429 reports a similar wrong fuel value (11160 g) at power on on vehicle 914 with OGCS 1.4.1. FS2-5043 has no content. No converted attachments.
